source.feature: Voice note → 3 idea packs (agencies in the AI era)
source.summary: 17-min voice dump → 9 ideas (see ideas.md). Top 3 turned into packs. Positioning leans 'AI infrastructure for agencies'; drafts keep the One Feature framing. SaaSSuite / yoursoftwareagent.com lines kept out.

claims: "6–12 months" timeline is Andrew's prediction; keep it framed as opinion.
items.linkedin:
I think basic marketing agencies have 6 to 12 months.

Not because they're bad. Because their clients are about to learn a new skill: using AI to use software.

If all you do is set up a CRM, build a website and manage it, the client will soon ask a fair question: why wouldn't I just ask Claude, or go to HighLevel directly?

But that doesn't mean agencies die. It means the job changes.

Therefore I'd focus on two things:

1. AI competency. The gap between what you can build with AI and what your client knows is your margin. Keep it wide.
2. Wrap it simpler. Most people will never go to HighLevel directly because it feels too complicated. Make it simple for them. That's the product.

The agencies that win won't sell software. They'll sell the gap.

items.feature: The reason they don't go direct is you
items.linkedin:
Every client of yours could go straight to the software.

They could open their own HighLevel account. Build their own website. Ask ChatGPT to set it up.

But most won't.

Nine times out of ten, the reason is you.

They want to text a person. They want to say "Rob's got it covered" and stop thinking about it. Even when the fix is simple, they want to know a human is behind it.

Therefore the human touch isn't a nice extra on top of your AI offer. It's the reason the offer exists.

Build the system. But stay the person they call.

items.feature: Sell the AI setup, not the tool
claims: Andrew says this is "often quite easy" but high value — keep pricing out until he gives a number.
items.linkedin:
Walk into a local restaurant and ask how they post on Facebook.

"Manually. When I remember."

You could show them an AI system that does it. You could even log them into one. But they'd use it for a week and stop.

Not because it's hard. Because they don't know what it can do.

That's the real gap. Not "how to use AI." What AI can take off their plate. Anything they do on a screen, an agent can probably handle.

And the setup won't become one-click anytime soon. Security, logins and permissions keep it complicated.

Therefore the opportunity is: build the AI setup for one kind of business, teach them what it can do, give them a simple chat to run it, and duplicate it.

One system. One niche. Then the next client.
